concepts.name: Satavahana Origins and Chronology
key_dimensions: Debate over founder — Simuka vs. Satakarni as the first king and the UPSC trap of conflating the two
Geographic origin controversy — Andhra Pradesh vs. Maharashtra (Pratishthan/Paithan as capital)
Chronological overlap with Kanva dynasty — how Satavahanas replaced Kanvas in the Deccan
Three phases of dynastic history: rise, decline under Sakas, and revival under Gautamiputra Satakarni

concepts.name: Gautamiputra Satakarni: Military Achievements and Titles
key_dimensions: Defeat of the Saka ruler Nahapana — numismatic evidence (restruck coins) as historical proof
Titles claimed in Nasik Prashasti — 'Ekabamhana' (upholder of Brahminical order), 'destroyer of Sakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas'
Contradiction in his rule: championed Brahminism yet gave land grants to Buddhist monks — UPSC trap on religious policy
His mother Gautami Balashri's Nasik inscription as a primary source — matrilineal naming convention significance

concepts.name: Satavahana Administrative Structure: Central and Provincial Governance
key_dimensions: Retention of Mauryan administrative units: Aharas (districts) equivalent to Mauryan Janapadas — comparison trap
Role of Amatyas and Mahamatras continued from Mauryan tradition versus new Satavahana-specific officials
Military governors — Senapatis as district administrators (unique Satavahana feature distinguishing them from purely civilian Mauryan officers)
Decentralized feudatory system: Rajas and Maharajas as subordinate chiefs — early sign of feudalism in Indian history

concepts.name: Satavahana Land Grant System and Its Socio-Political Implications
key_dimensions: Land grants to Brahmins and Buddhist monks — earliest systematic evidence of land grants in the Deccan
Concept of 'agrahara' villages granted to Brahmins with tax immunities — its role in spreading Brahminical culture southward
Alienation of fiscal and administrative rights along with land — proto-feudal implications
Distinction between royal land grants and merchant guild donations to Buddhist establishments — UPSC trap on who the donors were

concepts.name: Matrilineal Naming Convention in Satavahana Dynasty
key_dimensions: Kings identified by mother's name (e.g., Gautamiputra, Vasisthiputra) — unique feature among Indian dynasties
Debate: Does this indicate matrilineal descent or merely a naming convention honoring the mother? — UPSC conceptual trap
Cross-reference with Megasthenes' accounts of matrilineal communities in India
Contrast with contemporary dynasties (Kushanas, Sakas) where patrilineal naming was standard

concepts.name: Satavahana Social Structure and Varna System
key_dimensions: Satavahanas as 'dvija' (twice-born) — Brahminical claim vs. actual Shudra or mixed-varna origin debated by historians
Inscription evidence of mixed marriages across varnas — challenge to rigid varna orthodoxy
Role of guilds (shrenis) as a distinct social-economic class cutting across varna lines
Position of women: Inscriptional evidence of women making independent donations to Buddhist establishments

concepts.name: Satavahana Economy: Trade Networks and Coinage
key_dimensions: Control over strategic trade routes: Deccan plateau routes connecting western ports (Sopara, Kalyan) to eastern ports (Masulipatnam)
Satavahana coinage — predominantly lead and copper (not gold), significance of this for understanding economic hierarchy vs. Kushanas who issued gold coins
Bilingual and bilingual-script coins (Brahmi + local Prakrit) reflecting administrative pragmatism
Role of Satavahana trade in facilitating Roman trade through the Deccan — Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as a source

concepts.name: Satavahana Relationship with Sakas: Conflict and Cultural Synthesis
key_dimensions: Saka incursions weakening Satavahanas — Western Satraps (Kshatrapas) of Ujjain as the main antagonists
Vasisthiputra Pulumavi's matrimonial alliance with Saka ruler Rudradaman I — paradox of military conflict and dynastic marriage
Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription (oldest Sanskrit royal inscription) as evidence of Saka cultural assimilation vs. Satavahana Prakrit preference
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between Eastern Satraps and Western Satraps and their respective conflicts with Satavahanas

concepts.name: Satavahana Patronage of Buddhism and Rock-Cut Architecture
key_dimensions: Patronage of Karle, Bhaja, Nasik, and Kanheri chaityas and viharas — architectural features of each
Amaravati Stupa: Satavahana contributions — distinctive medallion style, 'Amaravati school' of sculpture
Paradox: Satavahanas claimed Brahminical identity yet were the largest patrons of Buddhist architecture — UPSC favorite conceptual contradiction
Nagarjunakonda as a later Buddhist center in Satavahana territory — distinction from Amaravati

concepts.name: Amaravati School of Art: Distinctive Features and Significance
key_dimensions: Distinctive use of white limestone ('Palnad marble') — contrast with Gandhara (schist) and Mathura (red sandstone)
Narrative style: dynamic, crowded compositions depicting Jataka stories vs. the more static Mathura style
Absence of anthropomorphic Buddha images in early phase — symbolic representation (footprints, wheel, empty throne)
Influence on Southeast Asian Buddhist art — cultural diffusion through maritime trade routes

concepts.name: Satavahana Language Policy and Contribution to Prakrit Literature
key_dimensions: Official use of Prakrit (not Sanskrit) in inscriptions — political and cultural significance of this choice
Hala's 'Gathasaptasati' (Sattasai) — anthology of Maharashtri Prakrit love poetry, its literary and social history value
Gunadhya's 'Brihatkatha' — lost work in Paisachi Prakrit, its influence on later Sanskrit literature (Kathasaritsagara)
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between Maharashtri Prakrit (literary), Ardhamagadhi (Jain), and Pali (Buddhist) — which was Satavahana official language

concepts.name: Role of Merchant Guilds (Shrenis) in Satavahana Economy and Culture
key_dimensions: Guilds as banking institutions — evidence of guild deposits bearing interest, used to fund temple rituals permanently
Guild donations to Buddhist caves — Nasik and Karle inscriptions naming specific guilds and occupations
Guilds as autonomous quasi-governmental bodies: internal governance, dispute resolution, and collective responsibility
Comparison with Mauryan guild system — Satavahana guilds had greater autonomy and cultural patronage role

concepts.name: Satavahana Port Cities and Maritime Trade
key_dimensions: Sopara, Kalyan (Kalliena in Periplus), and Bharuch (Barygaza) as western coast entrepôts under Satavahana influence
Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describing Satavahana king 'Balerour' (Vasisthiputra Pulumavi?) — source criticism angle
Export commodities: cotton textiles, spices, pearls, and iron — significance for Indo-Roman trade balance
UPSC trap: Distinguishing Satavahana-controlled ports from those controlled by Sakas and later Western Kshatrapas

concepts.name: Satavahana Inscriptions as Historical Sources
key_dimensions: Nasik Prashasti of Gautami Balashri — content, significance, and what it reveals about Gautamiputra's achievements
Nanaghat inscription — earliest known Satavahana inscription, mentioning yajnas (sacrifices) and royal donations
Limitation of inscriptions: mostly donative records, not administrative — gap in understanding day-to-day governance
Language of inscriptions: Prakrit in Brahmi script — contrast with contemporaneous Saka inscriptions in Sanskrit

concepts.name: Satavahana Religious Policy: Brahminism vs. Buddhism Patronage
key_dimensions: Performance of Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Rajasuya) by Satavahana kings — evidence from Nanaghat inscription
Simultaneous patronage of Buddhist monasteries and Brahminical agrahara grants — policy of strategic pluralism
Concept of 'Ekabamhana' title — protecting Brahminical social order while funding heterodox institutions
UPSC trap: Satavahanas are sometimes misclassified as exclusively Buddhist patrons — the Brahminical dimension is equally important

concepts.name: Feudatory System under Satavahanas and Origins of Feudalism in India
key_dimensions: Maharajas, Senapatis, and Mahasenapatis as feudatory chiefs — hierarchy of subordinate rulers
Grant of administrative immunities alongside land — fiscal decentralization as a structural feature
Comparison with later Gupta feudalism — Satavahana system as a precursor or prototype
Debate among historians (R.S. Sharma vs. critics) on whether Satavahana-era land grants truly represent 'feudalism' — UPSC historiography angle

concepts.name: Satavahana Contributions to Stupa Architecture: Sanchi and Amaravati
key_dimensions: Satavahana addition of toranas (gateways) to Sanchi Stupa — their iconographic program depicting Buddhist narratives
Distinction between the original Ashokan core of Sanchi and Satavahana-era additions — UPSC attribution trap
Amaravati Stupa's drum and railings — unique 'narrative friezes' technique vs. Sanchi's gateway narrative style
Loss and dispersal of Amaravati sculptures to British museums — historiographical and cultural heritage dimension

concepts.name: Decline of the Satavahana Empire: Causes and Successor States
key_dimensions: Internal fragmentation: rise of feudatory chiefs (Abhiras, Ikshvakus, Chutu Satakarnis) as successor states
External pressure: consolidation of Western Kshatrapas under Rudradaman permanently weakening Satavahana western territories
Economic decline: disruption of Roman trade from 3rd century CE reducing merchant guild prosperity
UPSC trap: Distinguishing successor states — Ikshvakus in Krishna-Guntur region (Buddhist patrons of Nagarjunakonda) vs. Vakatakas who are NOT direct Satavahana successors

concepts.name: Numismatic Evidence for Satavahana History
key_dimensions: Restruck Nahapana coins — direct evidence of Gautamiputra Satakarni's military victory, methodology of numismatic analysis
Lead coins as dominant Satavahana currency — what this indicates about the nature of trade (local vs. long-distance)
Bilingual coin legends in Prakrit and local scripts — evidence of administrative accommodation of regional diversity
Comparison with Kushana gold coins (dinara) — what the absence of gold coinage tells us about Satavahana vs. Kushana economic zones
